case_text: Serum from 30 participants was collected 28 days after a second dose of a recombinant vaccine containing a prefusion-stabilized glycoprotein from antigen lineage P. In a pseudovirus neutralization assay displaying the homologous full-length lineage P glycoprotein, 26 of 30 samples had ID50 values of at least 1:160. A separate IgG ELISA used an isolated receptor-binding domain from lineage Q that had been reduced, alkylated, and adsorbed to the plate. Twelve samples were below the ELISA lower limit of quantitation; 21 of 30 were below the assay's prespecified endpoint-titer response threshold of 1:400. No ELISA using the vaccine-matched, native-like trimer was reported.
final_answer: Most samples neutralized pseudovirus displaying the vaccine-matched lineage P glycoprotein, while the ELISA used a chemically treated, plate-bound receptor-binding domain from lineage Q. The mismatch in lineage and antigen presentation could produce low ELISA signal even when functional neutralizing antibodies are present. A matched native-like binding assay is needed to determine whether binding to the vaccine antigen is also low.
question_text: What could explain why most samples neutralize the homologous pseudovirus while many have low or unquantifiable binding in the reported ELISA?
evidence_linkage: The vaccine and pseudovirus both use lineage P, whereas the ELISA uses lineage Q, directly supporting an antigen-mismatch hypothesis. The ELISA antigen is also chemically treated and plate-adsorbed, unlike the full-length glycoprotein presented on pseudovirus, supporting a possible conformational or presentation effect. The reported results do not include a matched native-like binding assay, so they cannot show whether low ELISA signal reflects low overall binding or poor recognition of this particular ELISA reagent.
discordance_pattern: Neutralization was detected at ID50 values of at least 1:160 in 26 of 30 samples. In contrast, 12 of 30 ELISA results were below quantitation and 21 of 30 were below the ELISA response threshold. These results are discordant across assays with different antigen constructs, formats, and readouts.
explanatory_hypotheses: The ELISA antigen differs from the vaccine and pseudovirus antigens in both lineage and format. Lineage differences could reduce recognition of some vaccine-induced antibodies. Reduction and alkylation may disrupt conformational features recognized by antibodies that bind the prefusion glycoprotein, while plate adsorption may further alter epitope accessibility. The pseudovirus result demonstrates functional inhibition in its assay but does not establish how strongly those antibodies would bind the ELISA antigen.
assay_comparison_summary: The neutralization assay measured inhibition of pseudovirus bearing full-length lineage P glycoprotein, matching the vaccine lineage. The ELISA measured IgG binding to a reduced and alkylated isolated receptor-binding domain from lineage Q immobilized on a plate. Neutralization was reported as ID50, while ELISA results were endpoint titers with a separate response threshold.
preferred_interpretation: The reported ELISA is not a matched measure of binding to the vaccine-matched, native-like antigen. Its lineage and antigen-format differences provide a plausible explanation for low signal despite pseudovirus neutralization. The data support assay-specific discordance, but do not establish which antigen difference contributes most or quantify binding to the vaccine-matched trimer.
limitations_and_follow_up: The case lacks a lineage P native-like trimer ELISA, individual paired binding and neutralization values, and data on assay precision. Follow-up could test the same sera against lineage P and lineage Q antigens in matched, native-like formats, compare those results with the reduced and alkylated ELISA reagent, and repeat neutralization with appropriate controls. Such testing would help separate lineage effects from antigen-conformation and assay-format effects.

case_text: In a study of a recombinant vaccine containing an adjuvanted, prefusion-stabilized surface glycoprotein trimer, serum was collected from 24 participants 28 days after the second dose. An IgG ELISA using plates coated with the vaccine-matched trimer gave an endpoint-titer geometric mean of 1:25,600. In a pseudovirus neutralization assay using particles displaying the homologous full-length glycoprotein, the median ID50 was 1:45; 10 of 24 samples were below the assay's lower limit of quantitation of 1:20. Both assays used aliquots from the same collection visit. No epitope-mapping or native-cell-surface binding results were reported.
final_answer: The results show strong IgG binding to plate-coated recombinant trimer but limited functional neutralization in the pseudovirus assay. The binding response may contain antibodies that do not inhibit entry, and plate versus particle antigen presentation may also affect detection. The reported data do not distinguish these explanations, so binding titer alone should not be treated as a measure of neutralizing activity.
question_text: How should the high trimer-binding IgG titers and low pseudovirus neutralization results be interpreted?
evidence_linkage: The high ELISA titers establish substantial binding to the coated vaccine-matched trimer, but do not establish binding to the glycoprotein in its pseudovirus context or inhibition of entry. The low ID50 values directly indicate limited neutralization in that assay at the sampled time point. Use of the same visit and homologous glycoprotein reduces, but does not eliminate, explanations based on sample timing or antigen sequence mismatch. No epitope or native-surface data are available to distinguish non-neutralizing binding from presentation effects.
discordance_pattern: Binding titers were high in the ELISA, whereas neutralization was low overall: the pseudovirus median ID50 was 1:45 and 10 of 24 samples were below quantitation. The numerical titers are from different assay formats and are not directly comparable as a ratio.
explanatory_hypotheses: The binding response may include many antibodies that recognize the recombinant trimer but do not block the steps required for pseudovirus entry. Some ELISA-detected epitopes may be more accessible on plate-adsorbed antigen than on the glycoprotein displayed by pseudovirus. Differences in antibody avidity, concentration, or assay sensitivity could also contribute. The reported results do not identify which explanation predominates.
assay_comparison_summary: The ELISA measured IgG binding to plate-adsorbed, vaccine-matched recombinant trimer and reported endpoint titers. The pseudovirus assay measured inhibition of particles bearing the homologous full-length glycoprotein and reported ID50 values. The assays used aliquots from the same post-dose visit but differ in antigen presentation and measured function.
preferred_interpretation: The most defensible conclusion is that strong binding to the ELISA antigen did not translate into comparably strong pseudovirus neutralization in these samples. A substantial non-neutralizing component of the binding response is plausible, but assay-dependent epitope accessibility may also contribute; the available observations cannot separate these mechanisms.
limitations_and_follow_up: The case provides no individual-level relationship between ELISA and ID50 values, replicate precision, antibody isotypes, or epitope mapping. Useful follow-up would include repeat testing with documented assay controls, binding to glycoprotein displayed on cells or in a native-like format, competition or epitope-mapping assays, and an orthogonal neutralization assay. These measurements could clarify whether the gap reflects antibody specificity, antigen presentation, or assay performance.
